title: I split a ten year NQ backtest by hour, found the one hour holding the entire loss, filtered it out, and the result got $6,093 worse
author: person-person12
selftext:
This is a mistake I made last night and the numbers came out clean enough to be worth posting.

Setup: NQ, 5 minute candles, first 30 minutes of the session builds a range, first close outside it takes the break, one trade a day, both directions, stop 1 ATR, target 1 ATR, flat by 15:55. One contract from $50,000, May 2016 to August 2026. 2,562 trades, 49.9% wins, profit factor 0.96, finished at $26,259.

Then I grouped those same 2,562 trades by the hour the entry fired:

**14:00 UTC**, 1,269 trades, **+$14,159**, profit factor 1.05

**15:00 UTC**, 917 trades, **-$42,765**, profit factor 0.81

16:00 UTC, 225 trades, +$1,714, profit factor 1.04

everything later, 151 trades, +$3,150 between them

One bucket is more than the entire loss. So the fix looked obvious, only take the break inside the first hour after the range closes. I wrote that as a real rule, 60 minute window, changed nothing else, and ran the same ten years again.

**2,185 trades, 49.7% wins, profit factor 0.94, finished at $20,166.**

It removed 377 trades and came out **$6,093 worse** than leaving them in.

**\_\_\_\_\_**

The reason is daylight saving. Those buckets are UTC, and 14:00 UTC is 10am Eastern from March to November and 9am Eastern from November to March. A 9am Eastern entry cannot exist in this strategy because the range isnt finished until 10. So the summer 10am trades sat in the 14:00 bucket and the winter 10am trades sat in the 15:00 bucket, next to the summer 11am ones. The bucket I was going to delete was half the good trades wearing the wrong clock.

The genuinely late breaks, the 377 the window actually removed, made about +$6,100 between them.

**\_\_\_\_\_**

The thing doesnt work either way, and thats the bill rather than the clock. $25,620 of commission and slippage across 2,562 round turns at $2.50 a side and half a tick. Before costs the same trades made +3.76% over ten years, so the edge was worth roughly $1,900 gross and the execution came to thirteen times that.

I ran all of it in [Agenticks](https://www.agenticks.ca/?utm_source=reddit&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=autopilot&utm_content=ai_trading), which is mine, and grouping a result by hour is one click in there, which is exactly how easy it was to talk myself into cutting a fifth of the trades on a number that was not measuring what I read it as.

comments.author: SuperOrbital_Trading
comments.body: Lesson learned. Standardize all data sets to the same time zone.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: Agreed, and its worth checking even when youre sure everything is already sitting in one zone. In this one the hour bucket was correct, and the filter took out trades that were paying for the rest of the sample.

replies.author: SuperOrbital_Trading
replies.body: It is amazing how you can spend hours creating, versioning, verifying, and back testing and still end up with a loser because of some tiny little mistake. What is worse is hunting down an issue, fixing it, then still losing. So I feel ya. But, you can't make an omelet without cracking some eggs as the saying goes.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: Yea, and the worse version is when the fix is correct and the number still goes the wrong way, which is what happened here. Took me most of a day to accept that the hour I removed **wasnt the problem**.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body:
Good catch, and the DST bucketing trap goes beyond session-hour analysis. Anything anchored to an exchange or agency wall clock (the 9:30 ET open, 8:30 ET macro prints, 2:00 PM ET FOMC) moves in UTC twice a year, so any UTC-bucketed study quietly mixes two different regimes. The fix is to store event and bar times as timezone-aware timestamps in the source's local zone, bucket by that zone, and only convert to UTC for storage.

This matters even more for event-driven work. If you tag bars relative to a release time, a one-hour DST slip puts pre-release bars in the post-release window, and the backtest looks better for the wrong reason. It's the same discipline we've had to build into EventTrader at Cymetica: every event carries its canonical local release time plus a UTC equivalent, so windows stay aligned across DST.

Nice writeup on the sanity check, too. Deleting the "bad" bucket and seeing the result get worse is a cheap test everyone should run. [https://claude.ai/artifact/VuwYE2KYrtzMdwyEpvA9wH](https://claude.ai/artifact/VuwYE2KYrtzMdwyEpvA9wH)

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body:
Youre right, and the release version is the one that would have caught me out. My candle times are stored **timezone aware and bucketed in Eastern**, so the 9:30 open is still the 9:30 open through both flips, but I dont tag anything relative to a print yet.

How wide a window do you tag around a release before you call a candle post-event?
